children: IndiaFirst Life Insurance has generally been disciplined on expenses and commissions, so moving towards the 15 per cent threshold for Expense of Management (EoM), as proposed by IRDAI in its consultation paper, would not be particularly difficult for the company, says Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Rushabh Gandhi. In an interview with businessline, Gandhi says even for the life insurance company, however, extending the transition period from two years to three years would make the adjustment easier. Excerpts:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy Committee has shifted its stance from “neutral” to “calibrated tightening”. What change have you seen in consumer preferences since then?

We have not seen any meaningful change in consumer preferences. ULIPs have come down a bit, but that has more to do with market conditions than the policy stance. One shift, while not dramatic, has been encouraging. Following the GST waiver on pure protection policies, demand for term insurance has started moving in the right direction. Most industry participants believe the protection business will continue to grow, and that is core to our strategy as well.

For us, individual protection contributes a mid-single-digit share of individual annualised premium equivalent (APE). If we include PMJJBY (Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana), credit life and group term insurance, nearly 40 per cent of our business comes from protection. The balance comes from savings products.

The shift between participating (Par), non-participating (non-Par) and ULIP products is, in my view, temporary. Customer preference will continue to move with market conditions. When markets do well, ULIPs tend to see stronger demand. When markets are weak, they tend to lose some momentum. Retirement planning is also becoming increasingly important, and we expect annuities to be a significant growth driver going forward.
IndiaFirst Life Insurance’s current business mix is around 40 per cent protection and 60 per cent savings. Do you see this mix holding over the next two-three years?

PMJJBY should continue to grow because it remains a key focus area for the government. Individual protection is already on an upward trajectory, and we expect that trend to continue. Credit life is another important segment, although its growth will depend on how the proposed distribution reforms are implemented. The current proposal caps commissions at 2 per cent for single-premium products and 2.5 per cent in the first year for multi-year products.

If commissions remain at those levels, credit life could see some moderation. That said, any decline is likely to be offset by growth in PMJJBY and individual and group protection products. Overall, I don’t see the protection-savings mix changing materially over the next two to three years, though there could be some movement within the protection portfolio.

Industry players have submitted feedback to IRDAI on the proposed insurance distribution reforms. What is your view on the proposed commission cap for credit life products and the other proposals, particularly around expenses of management (EoM)?

Let me share our perspective on the proposals. These are my personal views and not necessarily those of the industry. On most aspects, there is broad alignment. Our feedback is limited to a few specific areas, including credit life commissions and the EoM transition path. Credit life is an important product because it protects a borrower’s outstanding loan obligations. A fair amount of work goes into integrating these products with lender’s systems and processes. It is also not automatically bundled with a loan; customers have to opt in.

At Bank of Baroda, for instance, borrowers who opt for a credit life policy receive a preferential interest rate on their home loan. Given the value such products provide, there may be a case for a somewhat higher commission cap than what has currently been proposed. That said, we respect the regulator’s approach.

For individual protection products sold on a single-premium basis, a commission cap of 7.5 per cent has been proposed. A similar cap for single-premium credit life would, in my view, strike a fair balance between the industry’s expectations and the regulator’s objectives. If an individual single-premium term plan can carry a 7.5 per cent commission, there is a rationale for applying the same benchmark to single-premium credit life products.

On expenses of management, directionally, the proposal is right and the 15 per cent threshold makes sense. The challenge is that only a handful of insurers currently operate below that level. A slightly longer glide path, say three years instead of two, would help. The regulator could also consider a different glide path for smaller and mid-sized insurers compared with larger players.

We have generally been disciplined on expenses and commissions, so moving towards the 15 per cent threshold would not be particularly difficult for us. Even for us, however, extending the transition period from two years to three would make the adjustment easier. More broadly, from an industry perspective, some differentiation may be worth considering.
In the consultation paper, commissions for Par, non-Par and ULIP products within the savings segment have been proposed at the same level. What is your view?

There is a case for a differentiated commission structure between ULIPs and traditional products because ULIPs are also subject to reduction-in-yield (RIY) considerations. A 20 per cent commission structure for ULIPs, while remaining within RIY limits, could make product design challenging. There may therefore be merit in moderating ULIP commissions.

At the same time, annuity products could be treated at par with Participating (Par) and non-Participating (non-Par) products. India does not have a comprehensive social security framework, and life expectancy continues to increase. Ensuring adequate retirement income is becoming increasingly important. People will have to save earlier and more consistently for retirement. Distributors also need adequate incentives to sell annuity products. From that perspective, there is a case for greater support for the annuity segment.
The proposed cuts in commissions have been particularly severe for insurance broking. Could the company’s distribution-channel mix change as a result?

In our case, broking accounts for about 10 per cent of business, and I do not expect that share to change materially. Large national brokers may find growth more challenging, but smaller, regional and local brokers are likely to continue expanding. As a result, the overall broking channel may not be significantly affected.

Today, any individual or company with ₹10 lakh can obtain a broking licence. Earlier, it was difficult for brokers to establish a presence across the country, but that is changing. So, while the overall contribution of broking is unlikely to change materially, some of the larger brokers could see a moderation in volumes.

Currently, bancassurance contributes around 65-70 per cent of our business, the agency channel around 15 per cent, and direct business about 8 per cent. If IRDAI’s proposed distribution norms are implemented in their current form, I expect direct business to grow. Beyond that, our strategy remains unchanged. We are, and will continue to be, a bancassurance-led, multi-channel insurer. Bancassurance is likely to remain our largest channel, although its contribution could moderate from 65-70 per cent to around 60-65 per cent over time. Direct business could increase to 13-14 per cent. We do not expect any dramatic shift in the overall channel mix.
We currently have around 20,000 agents across 100 branches and add nearly 2,000 agents every quarter. We expect that momentum to continue.

title: Extending EoM transition period to 3 years would make adjustment easier, says IndiaFirst Life Insurance MD & CEO
